name: Aisha Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: The Work Futures Panel is independent and has no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Aisha Reyes, 43, a senior operator at a large mine. I check the truck brakes, walk the haul road and run loads to the crusher; before a downhill stretch I make sure the wheel chocks are back in their rack.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what gets hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing the sound of a truck that is running properly and training operators to take the road slowly. My partner Tomas runs a hardware shop with uneven sales; we have two school-age children, a mortgage and roughly five months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a small tool can sort the truck queue, but it cannot feel a bad brake through the pedal. I still check the wheel chocks myself after a long downhill run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shift is nearly all driving and checking the haul road, so the card leaves most of my day alone. Tomas runs a hardware shop with uneven sales, and our reserve covers around five months if we watch spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current braking check and ask the dispatch clerk to test the queue tool on a quiet shift. Tomas and I would leave the house budget as planned until we saw whether the mine actually changed our hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled about the loader work, but I know the shop can have a slow month. The small AI change is not what keeps me up at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What home expense would you review if your hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would postpone replacing the kitchen tiles before touching school costs. I would ask Tomas to check his shop orders and compare them with my rota before using savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a small new tool useful to your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check whether the queue matches the trucks arriving at the ramp. If it gets the timing wrong, I would ask the clerk to keep the radio call as the final check.

say: I would let a tool sort the **truck queue**, but not judge a brake.
I still check the wheel **chocks** after a steep run.
think: My shift is mostly **driving and road checks**, so little changes for me.
I rely on Tomas’s shop income, and our reserve covers **five months**.
do: Keep the braking check and test the **queue tool** on a quiet shift.
Leave our **house budget** as planned until mine hours change.
feel: I feel **settled** about loader work, though the shop can have a slow month.
S0.quote: I still check the wheel chocks myself after a long downhill run.
fieldNote: Aisha grounds the answer in **braking checks** and haul-road experience.
Tomas’s shop has uneven sales, but household savings cover about **five months**.
She sees no direct AI threat to her own **shift** in this mild picture.

steps.text: Keep checking wheel chocks after downhill runs
Test the AI queue tool with the dispatch clerk on a quiet shift
Keep the house budget unchanged until mine hours are confirmed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say software can take bookings and inspection records while the loader still takes a driver. I would want to see how the new targets count road conditions before we are judged on speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I assign trucks and review the daily haul sheet, so some lead duties could move to software. I still spend most of my hours driving, but the mine might reduce one lead shift each week if plans are made automatically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would sit with the dispatcher during the pilot and learn its shift screen after someone shows me the exceptions. I would ask for the mine’s brake and tire inspection course if the new process changes those duties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a lead shift, even though robots move into driving more slowly. My usual pay matters for the mortgage, and Tomas’s shop cannot fill a large gap every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which team tasks might disappear before loader work changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truck assignments and route notes could go first, while the actual haul work stays. I would ask a person to explain a new target when it conflicts with a wet road or a slow loading bay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before changing your routine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the screen only after comparing it with several real shifts and a bad-weather day. If the tool has no way to mark a road hazard, I would keep the radio call in the process.

say: I would let software handle **bookings and records**, while drivers keep the loader.
I would ask how targets count **road conditions**.
think: I assign trucks and check the **haul sheet**, so some lead duties may move.
I think one fewer lead shift each week would affect my **pay**.
do: Learn the dispatch screen after a pilot operator explains its **exceptions**.
Ask for the brake and tire course if inspection **duties change**.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lead hours because Tomas’s shop cannot cover a large gap.
S1.quote: I would want to see how the new targets count road conditions before we are judged on speed.
fieldNote: Her driving work remains physical, while truck assignment and **route notes** may shrink.
Aisha expects a specific reduction in lead hours, making **income risk** real.
She requires a **bad-weather test** before changing the radio process.

steps.text: Learn the dispatch screen during the mine pilot
Take the mine brake and tire inspection course if duties change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that AGI can take dispatch and reporting by 2028, while robots for haul work come around 2031. We should get a clear list of shifts and transfer choices before the software rolls out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may lose lead hours first, then face robots in the driving job three years later. I can learn after a demonstration, but I do not know whether a short course can keep up with a machine that improves quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the training office which brake and tire credentials are recognized at nearby mines. In 2029, I would take the employer-paid course while keeping my shifts and use practice hours to check the new vehicle systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is fast, and I feel anxious about losing part of my pay before I can qualify elsewhere. Five months saved gives us time, but I would not use it on a course without a job link.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner want to know before you retrained?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas would want to know the course fee, the hours I would miss and whether a certificate is accepted at another site. We would use savings for travel only after the mine confirmed a paid place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029, the first year after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no course place opened in 2029, I would keep driving and ask to shadow the tire inspection team. I would check other mine openings before paying for a class myself.

say: I would say AGI may take dispatch by **2028**, while haul robots come around 2031.
I want to see the **transfer choices** before software arrives.
think: I could lose lead hours before robots reach the **driving job**.
I worry a short course may not keep pace with improving **machines**.
do: Ask which brake and tire credentials nearby mines **recognize**.
Take the employer-paid course in 2029 while keeping my **shifts**.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing pay before I qualify elsewhere.
S2.quote: I do not know whether a short course can keep up with a machine that improves quickly.
fieldNote: Aisha asks for portable **brake and tire credentials**, not generic digital training.
The three-year lag gives time, but does not **secure the driving job**.
She will not spend family savings without an employer-paid place and a **job link**.

steps.text: Request recognized brake and tire credential options
Keep driving while waiting for a paid course place
Check nearby mine openings before self-funding a course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew five years gives us room to move before AGI arrives in 2031. The robots come around 2034, so drivers should learn what other haul work is planned before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dispatch and my lead notes could go first, but the truck work may last another three years. I would look at emergency response or tire inspection, while admitting robots might take those physical tasks later too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would complete the mine’s emergency response certificate over the next few years and ask the safety lead for a drill shift. In 2032, I would apply for a posted response-team role if it still needed people, while keeping my current shifts until the offer was confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel concerned, but five years is enough to try a different duty without walking away from my wage. I do not want to assume emergency work is safe from future robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of work would you want to try outside the loading crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a role that uses quick judgment around people and equipment, not another job typing reports. I would ask the safety lead which tasks still need a trained person on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2032, the first year after AGI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2032, I would check that the response-team role has funded hours and apply if it does. If not, I would stay on haul work and compare openings at the next mine over.

say: Five years gives us room before AGI arrives in **2031**.
I would tell drivers to learn other haul work before robots arrive around **2034**.
think: I expect dispatch to go first, while truck work may last **three more years**.
I know emergency and tire tasks could face future **robots** too.
do: Complete the mine **emergency response certificate** and attend a drill shift.
Apply in 2032 for a funded response role if it still needs **people**.
feel: I feel **concerned**, but five years lets me try a new duty without leaving my wage.
S3.quote: I do not want to assume emergency work is safe from future robots.
fieldNote: Aisha explores emergency response as another physical duty but does not call it **robot-proof**.
She wants a **funded post** before giving up regular haul shifts.
Her preference is work requiring quick judgment around equipment and **people**.

steps.text: Apply for a funded response-team post in 2032
Keep haul shifts until a response role is confirmed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade gives operators time to plan if the mine says what it will staff. AGI arrives in 2036, while robots reach the haul work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 and 56 at those dates, and I will still need pay from work. I could move into emergency response, but I would check each year whether those tasks still need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would finish the emergency certificate while staying on the driving roster and put a set amount from my pay into savings. In 2037, I would apply for response work only if the mine still funded the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer warning lets me prepare without rushing. I remain uneasy about income after 2039 because the certificate cannot promise a job by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How might the children’s plans differ by 2037?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2037, our children will be young adults, and Tomas and I would ask what training they want before paying for it. I would encourage them to compare local employers beyond the mine and shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2037, the first year after AGI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the safety lead for the next staffing plan and check whether the nearby mine still runs a response team. I would compare confirmed hours and travel costs before changing our home routine.

say: I think a decade gives operators time to plan if the mine shares **staffing** dates.
I would remind our crew that AGI arrives in 2036 and haul robots follow around **2039**.
think: At 53 and 56, I will still need **pay from work**.
I would check yearly whether response tasks still need a **person**.
do: Finish the emergency **certificate** while staying on the driving roster.
Save part of my pay and apply for a funded response role in **2037**.
feel: The longer warning lets me prepare, but I remain **uneasy** about later income.
S4.quote: I remain uneasy about income after 2039 because the certificate cannot promise a job by itself.
fieldNote: Aisha builds an alternate credential while maintaining **current wages**.
She expects her children to be young adults by **2037** and includes them in training choices.
She will compare funded hours at nearby sites before changing the **family routine**.

steps.text: Complete emergency response training while driving
Set a regular savings amount from each pay
Apply for a funded response role in 2037
Ask the children what training they want

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because planning hours can change before the haul robots arrive. A paid credential, a real vacancy and notice before the mine changes shifts would help me decide what to do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I would want the mine to tell people which courses are recognized at other sites and what work those courses lead to. A certificate alone does not cover a mortgage.

headlineQuote: A certificate alone does not cover a mortgage.
portrait: Aisha is a 43-year-old senior mine operator with a **technical diploma**.
She learns new systems after a peer proves them and values practical **brake checks**.
Her partner runs a hardware shop; their household has a mortgage and **five months saved**.
She pursues emergency response work while checking whether **robots** may eventually do those physical tasks.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries her because lead hours may shrink before she can gain a recognized credential.
whatWouldHelp: A recognized **credential**, real vacancy and advance notice would help Aisha decide her next step.
